title: Victim faced charges for earlier cop attack
article: A Sudanese immigrant killed early Saturday by a Calgary cop was wanted by police at the time of his death after allegedly assaulting another city officer earlier this year.
Deng Fermino Kuol, 34, was also wanted by RCMP in Brooks for breach of probation after a drunk driving conviction. He'd previously been convicted of assault in the southern Alberta town.
Police in Brooks, 185 kilometres southeast of Calgary, said Kuol was well-known to officers and was often violent.
"He was an individual that was known to police, and our members would use caution when dealing with him," said Brooks RCMP Staff Sgt. Ray Noble.
Noble explained that when attending calls where officers were aware Kuol was involved, "You'd make sure you had two (police) vehicles going."

A provincial court judge in Calgary issued a warrant for Kuol's arrest on Oct. 14 after he failed to appear to face charges of assaulting a peace officer and not complying with a probation order to abstain from drinking alcohol, court documents show.
It was alleged that on June 2, Kuol assaulted Const. L. Garry Basso, a veteran officer assigned to District 4.
Const. Ira Macumber, the officer who shot and killed Kuol early Saturday, worked at the same station.
Kuol, an unemployed meat packer, was shot by Macumber around 12:30 a.m. Saturday, after a struggle outside an apartment building at 1709 37th St. S.E.
Kuol was sitting outside the residence when the police officer arrived. Investigators said that after initially agreeing to leave, Kuol drew a knife and slashed the officer in the left bicep.
Macumber struggled to restrain his attacker, then pulled his gun and fired twice -- in keeping with officer training, according to police.
The incident sparked a bitter debate between members of the Sudanese community and police.
The Calgary medical examiner's office confirmed Monday that Kuol died as a result of two gunshot wounds to the neck.
Macumber, just moments before the shooting, was stabbed in the arm by Kuol during a struggle on what initially seemed to be a routine eviction.

Friends and family of the dead man have come out in support of Kuol, accusing police of using excessive force. They are angry Macumber shot Kuol in the neck instead of aiming for his legs or arms -- a wound that would disable him.
They also denied Kuol was carrying a weapon.
"He never carried a knife in his life," said brother Bol Agot from his home in Brooks.
Agot admitted Kuol was a heavy drinker who became a "different person" when under the influence.
His drinking began after a failed relationship with an old girlfriend in Brooks, Agot said.

Edna Sutherland, executive director of the Calgary Immigrant Women's Association, said the incident has caused friction between police and the 7,500-member Sudanese community, but they will rebuild the relationship.
"(Their) first response is denial, but they are going to have to accept this," Sutherland said of the Sudanese community. "They certainly want to wait for the full investigation and get the facts."
Sutherland has been chosen to represent the Sudanese community in dealings with police.
One of Calgary's top officers said he doesn't question Macumber's actions.

"I would never second guess an officer who makes the decision under the circumstances. In this case, where in doing your job you're attacked by someone wielding a knife, who stabs you. You're fearing for your life," said Deputy Chief Rick Hanson.
"If someone was stabbing me and I knew that person was trying to kill me, I'm trying to eliminate the threat."
Hanson said the police service fully expects to be scrutinized by the public, and especially by the Sudanese community.

He said even though in this case police officers are investigating police officers, the Crown prosecutor's office and a pending public fatality inquiry will ensure all details are revealed. As for Macumber's decision to shoot Kuol instead of using pepper spray, Hanson said other options don't always work.

"It's easy to say that an alternative method of force could have been effective," he said. "It's a fact that not everybody responds to pepper spray. It's also a fact that Tasers are not effective in all cases."
Alberta Solicitor General Heather Forsyth said she also supports Macumber and will contact him soon.
"He needs to know that I understand the situation he was in," she said. "(Police officers) are sworn to saving people's lives, not taking them."
Calgary police Chief Jack Beaton said Monday he believes there was no other way of quelling the situation but to shoot Kuol.
"It was a life-threatening situation," said Beaton. "(Macumber's) life was in jeopardy."
The investigation into the shooting is expected to take two weeks.
